verdict:
This is a quiet, procedural first-contact novel set at a small US Antarctic research station (Winslow) during June 1991, told from the perspective of a single winterover scientist who detects an anomalous radio signal and spends twelve days protecting degrading evidence in isolation. The implicit contract it asks a verisimilitude reader to accept is stringent: 1991 Antarctic technology and institutional structures, electromagnetic physics, magnetic tape degradation chemistry, diesel generator behaviour under cold, and scientific epistemology. Against that contract, the book pays its debts on nearly every page. The LC-130 Hercules on ski struts, the Single Sideband radio net, the USAP relay-window structure, the INTELSAT arc gone below the southern horizon, the thermal paper printout whose ink fractures in sustained cold — all of it is rendered with the authority of genuine research or first-hand knowledge. The diesel viscosity correction in Chapter 05 is exactly right. The binder-stress failure mode for cold-stored magnetic tape (oxide separation at the reel edge, sharp dropout onset, progression toward the primary recording track) is technically coherent throughout.

Two specific errors are concentrated in a single paragraph of Chapter 07 and appear to share a common cause. Elena's internal monologue reads: "Forty-seven seconds on the secondary UHF band, fourteen minutes before her detection, at a propagation geometry consistent with a common source. Two stations, two instruments, two frequency bands, a timing offset that matched the propagation delay at sixty kilometers." At this point in the narrative (Day 7), Elena has not received Lars's precise data: on Day 3 he told her his event lasted "about a minute, perhaps slightly less" and occurred "last week." The specific figure of forty-seven seconds and the fourteen-minute offset are data Lars gives her only in Chapter 10 ("Duration: forty-seven seconds" and the 2208 timestamp). Elena cannot know these numbers on Day 7. The second error is in the same sentence: a fourteen-minute timing offset between two stations sixty kilometres apart cannot "match the propagation delay at sixty kilometres" for electromagnetic radiation. Light covers sixty kilometres in 0.0002 seconds; a fourteen-minute offset is geometrically consistent with a directed signal sweeping from east to west, not with propagation delay. Both errors most likely originated when the author, having already worked out the Chapter 10 data, revised Chapter 07 without tracking the information boundary — Elena was inadvertently given foreknowledge. The same Lars-timeline pressure produces a smaller error in Chapter 03, where Lars describes his June 1 reading as having occurred "last week" in a contact that takes place on June 3 — two days later, not a week.

A third concrete defect is numerical: in Chapter 11, Elena lists the dropout progression as "five seconds confirmed on Run 3, Day 4. Eight seconds estimated by visual inspection on Days 6 and 7. Twelve seconds confirmed on Run 4, Day 8." But Chapter 09 is explicit that Run 4 produced eight seconds of first-segment silence — the twelve seconds was the second parametric segment gap, a distinct and newly discovered failure pathway. Chapter 12 confirms the separation: Run 5 shows a "reel-edge interval" of approximately nine seconds (first segment, +1 from Run 4's 8) and a "gap" of twenty seconds (second segment, growing from Run 4's 12). Chapter 11's "Eighteen seconds now" visual estimate for what it calls the first-segment progression is also irreconcilable with Run 5's nine seconds the following morning. The chapter has silently conflated two different degradation measurements, producing a progression table whose middle and terminal values are borrowed from the wrong instrument reading. A reader tracking Elena's numbers against the instrument logs will catch this. Against these specific findings, the remaining twelve chapters are largely clean. The book earns its technical register and is, by any fair standard, exceptionally well-grounded for this kind of work.

strongest.claim: Antarctic period detail is accurate and dense throughout: LC-130 ski-equipped Hercules transport, Single Sideband radio with the USAP relay-window structure, INTELSAT arc positions, thermal paper printout limitations, fax as the transmission medium, diesel fuel viscosity under extreme cold. These specifics are all authentic to early-1990s Antarctic station operations and none are contradicted.

Magnetic tape degradation physics is technically coherent: binder stress confined to the reel edge at the maximum circumference, the oxide-layer separation producing sharp (not gradual) dropout onset, and the independent internal binder failure at the second parametric segment as a distinct pathway from the reel-edge progression. The loupe examination method and the tape-speed-to-time calculation are both plausible field procedures.

Elena's epistemic discipline is consistent across all fifteen chapters. She refuses every softening formulation ('She was not going to write *ruled out* and mean *probably ruled out*'), tracks every number with an attached method and a stated uncertainty, and distinguishes a provisional claim from a confirmed one with the precision the story's stakes require. This character property never slips.

Generator fault behaviour and fuel arithmetic are technically sound: voltage regulator variance widening under prolonged cold, the stabilization procedure via load-shedding, the diesel viscosity correction at -28°C (thickening, not yet wax-crystal gelling — correctly distinguished from the colder threshold), and the power-reserve accounting maintained across all twelve days without internal contradiction.

weakest.claim: Chapter 07 (Day 7) has Elena thinking 'Forty-seven seconds on the secondary UHF band, fourteen minutes before her detection' as known fact — but she does not receive Lars's precise duration or timestamp until the Chapter 10 contact (Day 9). On Day 7 she knows only 'about a minute, perhaps slightly less' and 'last week.' The specific figures are a narrative anachronism, most likely an artifact of the author knowing the Chapter 10 data while revising Chapter 07.

The same Chapter 07 paragraph states 'a timing offset that matched the propagation delay at sixty kilometers.' Electromagnetic radiation covers sixty kilometres in roughly 0.0002 seconds; a fourteen-minute timing offset cannot match that propagation delay by any reading of the physics. The correct framing — a directed signal whose beam arrived at each station sequentially — appears in Chapter 10 and Chapter 12 without this error, which suggests Chapter 07 was not updated when the author found the cleaner formulation.

Chapter 11 records the first-segment dropout progression as 'five seconds confirmed on Run 3, Day 4. Eight seconds estimated by visual inspection on Days 6 and 7. Twelve seconds confirmed on Run 4, Day 8.' But Chapter 09 establishes that Run 4 produced eight seconds of first-segment silence; the twelve seconds was the second parametric segment gap, a separate and newly discovered failure. Chapter 12 (Run 5) confirms the separation: 'reel-edge interval ~9s' (first segment) versus a 'gap' of twenty seconds (second segment). Chapter 11's 18-second visual estimate for the first segment is irreconcilable with Run 5's nine seconds the next morning.

Lars says 'Last week I had some anomalous instrument readings' in the Day 3 contact. His event is subsequently confirmed (Chapter 10) to have occurred on June 1 — two days before the Day 3 contact (June 3), not the previous week. The inconsistency is small but traceable, and it is the same Lars-timeline pressure that produces the larger Chapter 07 anachronism.

The SSB contact with Mather Station (sixty kilometres east) is described as carrying 'the flutter that sixty kilometres of ionospheric path introduced at these latitudes.' At sixty kilometres, HF/SSB propagates primarily by ground wave, which is stable and flutter-free; ionospheric sky-wave effects dominate at much greater distances. Polar winter conditions complicate this, but the description confidently attributes the flutter to ionospheric propagation for a path where ground wave should dominate.

quotes.text: She was not going to write *ruled out* and mean *probably ruled out*.
quotes.why: Establishes Elena's epistemic standard at the outset; the rest of the book is judged against this line, and it holds — which is what makes the Chapter 07 lapse in information discipline more damaging.

quotes.text: Forty-seven seconds on the secondary UHF band, fourteen minutes before her detection, at a propagation geometry consistent with a common source.
quotes.why: Elena states as known fact both the 47-second figure and the 14-minute offset — data she does not receive from Lars until the Chapter 10 contact two days later. The anachronism is in this sentence.

quotes.text: a timing offset that matched the propagation delay at sixty kilometers
quotes.why: The propagation delay for electromagnetic radiation across sixty kilometres is approximately 0.0002 seconds, not fourteen minutes. This is the physics error in the same paragraph.

quotes.text: Blank oxide meant the magnetic coating had failed in that region.
quotes.why: Exact and correct; distinguishes total oxide loss from partial dropout or noise, supporting the book's claim that the second parametric segment is unrecoverable. The tape physics is right here.

quotes.text: Twelve seconds confirmed on Run 4, Day 8.
quotes.why: Chapter 09 shows Run 4 produced eight seconds of first-segment silence; twelve seconds was the second-segment gap. This figure belongs to the wrong measurement in the progression table.

quotes.text: Last week I had some anomalous instrument readings
quotes.why: Lars's event is confirmed in Chapter 10 to have occurred on June 1; this contact is June 3 — two days earlier, not last week. A small error but part of the same Lars-timeline inconsistency cluster.

quotes.text: The ski struts came down on the second approach — she could see the shape change at the fuselage at this altitude
quotes.why: The LC-130 Hercules used ski-wheel landing gear for Antarctic operations; the observation that the strut deployment is visible from the strip is consistent with the aircraft's approach altitude. The period detail is exact.

put_down_points: Chapter 04–05: the compound fuel-arithmetic over two consecutive chapters — power-gauge percentages, fuel-litre calculations, burn-rate corrections, parallel tracking counts — is dense enough that a reader not engaged with the technical problem-solving may skim, particularly since the emotional stakes are not directly foregrounded during the arithmetic.

Chapter 11: the printout column-by-column examination runs to detailed but static inventory; any reader who has already accepted that the document is degrading may find the granularity of the damage catalogue (fractured characters recoverable by context, mosaic fracture structure, oblique-light photography) slows momentum without adding proportionate dramatic weight.
who_is_this_for: Readers who responded to Kim Stanley Robinson's Antarctica (1997) or the engineering problem-solving register of The Martian, but who want that precision applied to a quieter, more morally complex situation. Also: anyone drawn to first-contact stories handled with scientific restraint rather than spectacle; readers interested in the ethics of scientific communication and institutional capture of findings; people who find Antarctic isolation literature compelling in its own right. This book requires patience with procedural repetition and rewards close attention to numbers.
